Monmouth County by the numbers

Where is Monmouth County, NJ, and how is it laid out?

Monmouth County occupies the central coast of New Jersey, bordered by Middlesex and Mercer Counties to the west, Ocean County to the south, the Atlantic Ocean to the east and Raritan Bay to the north. Wikipedia reports 661.40 square miles in total, but only 468.18 are land, because 29.2% of the county's area is water.

Freehold Borough is the county seat, although many county offices also sit in neighboring Freehold Township. Middletown Township is the most populous municipality, with 67,106 residents in 2020, and Howell Township is the largest by area at 61.21 square miles. The county holds fifty-three municipalities, according to the ranking listed for Middletown on Wikipedia.

The land is mostly low and flat. Hills rise around Holmdel, where Crawford Hill is the county's highest point at roughly 380 to 391 feet, and in the Locust section of Middletown and the boroughs of Highlands and Atlantic Highlands. The shore towns, from Long Branch and Asbury Park down to Spring Lake, set the market for oceanfront homes, while western towns such as Freehold, Marlboro and Colts Neck are inland and more rural.

Who handles property tax in Monmouth County?

Municipal offices send the bills. Each of the county's towns has its own assessor and tax collector, and the Monmouth County Board of Taxation oversees assessments and hears appeals. The board's assessment information page gives its address as the Hall of Records, 1 East Main Street, Freehold, NJ 07728, and its phone number as (732) 431-7404.

How the board works, per its own page:

  • Five members are appointed by the governor.
  • The board hears assessment disputes, and the municipality is represented by its attorney.
  • All of its meetings are public.

The county also offers a property tax estimator through its record search, and the Township of Middletown's page points owners to that tool for projecting a bill.

For a payoff before closing, call the collector for the town where the house stands. Your title company will ask that town's tax office for the figure.

What makes the Monmouth County appeal calendar different?

Monmouth follows an alternate assessment calendar, and the tax appeal deadline is January 15 rather than April 1. The New Jersey Division of Taxation names Monmouth, Burlington and Gloucester as the three counties on that calendar in its appeal guide. Hearings are generally held after the January 15 deadline, and the board generally denies adjournments.

The county's appeal page adds these details:

  • An assessment is presumed correct, so the owner must prove it is excessive or discriminatory.
  • Evidence should relate to the October 1 assessment date, and at least three comparable sales go to the assessor, the clerk and the tax board a week before the hearing if they were not filed with the petition.
  • All taxes and municipal charges through the first quarter must be paid to the collector.
  • Owners of income-producing property must supply an income statement on the board's forms.
  • A skipped hearing leads to dismissal for lack of prosecution.

A dissatisfied owner has 45 days from the mailing of the judgment to appeal to the Tax Court of New Jersey. If the assessment is over $1,000,000, the owner can file directly with the Tax Court by April 1. The board also explains the Chapter 123 test: when the ratio of assessment to true value exceeds the average ratio by more than 15%, the assessment is reduced to the common level.

How does annual reassessment work in Monmouth County?

Monmouth took part in an Assessment Demonstration Program created by P.L. 2013, c. 15, which moved the county toward more frequent reassessment. Middletown's assessment page cites a Monmouth University study that found both vertical and horizontal inequity in residential assessments dropped after the program began, and notes that the county's assessors association and tax board received a 2019 Distinguished Jurisdiction Award from the International Association of Assessing Officers.

For owners, that history has a practical effect. Values are updated more often, so a change in the assessment notice reflects recent sales instead of waiting for a one-time revaluation. Middletown reported that its aggregate preliminary net value for tax year 2026 was 7.94% above 2025 and that the rate was expected to fall as a result. An owner can look up property record cards, sales data and prior postcards in the county's online record search before deciding to appeal.

What do Census figures say about Monmouth County homes?

Monmouth is a wealthy, owner-heavy county with an older population than Middlesex. The table draws on Census QuickFacts and covers the 2020-2024 period unless noted.

Monmouth County housing and income measures from Census QuickFacts
MeasureMonmouth County
Population, 2020 Census643,615
Population estimate, July 2025651,035
Owner-occupied housing rate75.6%
Median value of owner-occupied homes$606,100
Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage$3,070
Median household income$124,845
Persons 65 and over21.4%
Building permits, 20252,138

With more than a fifth of residents over 65, Monmouth sees plenty of sales by longtime owners, heirs and downsizers.

How has the shore shaped Monmouth County property values?

Hurricane Sandy in 2012 hit the northern Jersey Shore hard, and Wikipedia reports that whole neighborhoods in Monmouth County were demolished and rebuilt, some at a higher price level than before. The page ties that rebuilding to rising values in many shore communities and to purchases by buyers seeking second homes near New York.

The county's economy reaches beyond the beach. The Bell Labs Holmdel complex became a business incubator in 2016, Freehold Raceway Mall is a super-regional shopping center, and Pier Village in Long Branch anchors the oceanfront. The county's gross domestic product was $34.2 billion in 2021. For a seller, a location on the water or near a train line sets much of the price, and the assessor's record for your lot sets the tax.

What relief programs can Monmouth County owners use?

The state offers relief that applies in every county. The Division of Taxation's relief page says the fiscal year 2027 budget funds the Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ programs, and that the 2025 application deadline was November 2, 2026. Local assessors handle the senior, disabled and veteran deductions on the municipal side. In Middletown, for example, the assessor's office assists with senior and veteran relief and with a review of a property record card.

A sale during the year may change eligibility, so ask the state program office how a mid-year move affects a claim before you close.

More questions about Monmouth County, NJ Property Tax Guide

What is the Monmouth County property tax appeal deadline?

January 15. Monmouth uses an alternate assessment calendar, and the statewide April 1 date does not apply to most owners. An assessment over $1,000,000 can go directly to the Tax Court by April 1.

How do I contact the Monmouth County Board of Taxation?

Call (732) 431-7404 or write to the County Board of Taxation, Hall of Records, 1 East Main Street, Freehold, NJ 07728. The board can send the forms needed to file an assessment appeal.

What if I disagree with the Monmouth County Tax Board's decision?

You have 45 days from the date the judgment was mailed to file a further appeal with the Tax Court of New Jersey. Missing a hearing leads to dismissal for lack of prosecution, which can block that next step.

Can I appeal my Monmouth County property tax bill itself?

No. Taxes come from local budgets and cannot be appealed. You can challenge only the assessment, and you must pay all taxes and municipal charges through the first quarter while the appeal is pending.

How many comparable sales do I need for a Monmouth County appeal?

Submit at least three comparable sales. The board wants them delivered to the assessor, the clerk and the tax board at least a week before the hearing if they were not attached to the petition.

Morris County by the numbers

Which offices run property tax inside Morris County?

Morris County splits the job between a county board and 39 town offices. The Morris County Board of Taxation holds the county's records of taxable real estate, sets tax rates and equalization ratios, supervises the municipal assessors, reviews assessments and rules on appeals. Its mailing address is P.O. Box 900, Morristown, NJ 07963-0900.

New Jersey leaves budgets to local government, and the state receives none of the property tax money. A town divides the dollars it must raise by the assessed value of everything taxable inside its borders, and that quotient is the general rate. Your bill equals the rate times your own assessment (NJ Division of Taxation).

  • Your town's assessor sets the number printed on your notice.
  • The county board hears disputes about that number and publishes each town's rate.
  • The Morris County Clerk files the deed once the house closes.

How pricey and how owner heavy are Morris County homes?

Morris County is wealthy and mostly owner occupied. Census QuickFacts puts the 2025 population estimate at 524,251, up from 509,285 in the 2020 count, with 193,245 households averaging 2.62 people. Morris County is a stable place to live: 91.1 percent of residents were in the same house a year earlier.

Morris County housing facts, Census QuickFacts (survey years 2020 to 2024 unless noted)
MeasureMorris County figure
Housing units, 2025 estimate202,261
Owner occupied housing unit rate74.3%
Typical owner's home value$582,500
Monthly owner cost, mortgaged$3,295
Monthly owner cost, no mortgage$1,385
Median gross rent$1,904
Median household income$137,326
Building permits issued, 20251,324

Owners without a mortgage still carry $1,385 a month, and a large share of that is the tax bill and insurance. About 57.8 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree, and the mean commute is 29.8 minutes.

What does the Morris County landscape mean for a seller?

The county lies roughly 30 miles west of New York City and is run from Morristown, with commuter towns throughout and no big city. Parsippany-Troy Hills is the most populous municipality at 56,162 people in 2020, and Rockaway Township covers the most ground at 45.55 square miles. Roughly 4.3 percent of the county's 481.52 square miles is water.

The land climbs from the flatter Passaic River valley suburbs in the east to hills in the west. The highest point, 1,395 feet, is in western Jefferson Township. The Rockaway River drains 125 square miles of the north, the Whippany River drains 69 square miles through the middle, and the South Branch of the Raritan and the Black River drain the west. Drainage differs between valley floor and ridge, so ask your town's office whether the lot sits near a mapped flood area before you set a price.

The housing stock carries history. The Continental Army wintered at Jockey Hollow in 1779 and 1780, and Dover was an iron mining center in the 1880s. Older houses in places like these tend to need more work, and the gap shows up in what buyers offer for a house sold as it stands. The county's per capita income was the highest in New Jersey in 2021, which keeps renovation expectations high.

How do I contest a Morris County assessment?

The Morris County Board of Taxation must receive your petition by April 1, with May 1 applying in a town that has just revalued or reassessed. The Division of Taxation's form A-1 and the comparable sales sheet go in together (NJ Division of Taxation).

The county board holds that your value counts as excessive only when it misses a yardstick. After a revaluation, the yardstick is 100 percent of market value on the previous October 1. In other years, the town's common level range is the yardstick, set at plus or minus 15 percent around its average ratio.

  • Use arm's length sales dated before October 1.
  • Plan to appear in person, because the board runs no virtual hearings.
  • If the board's judgment disappoints you, the Tax Court of New Jersey is the next stop, with a 45 day clock.
  • An assessment over $1,000,000 gives the owner a choice to bypass the county board.
  • Added or omitted assessments use form AA-1, with direct Tax Court access above $750,000.

Which relief programs end when a Morris County owner sells?

Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ attach to a principal residence, which means a sale ends them for that address. An owner aged 65 or older may qualify for all three, and a renter qualifies for ANCHOR only. The state's posted application deadline was November 2, 2026, and it has passed (Division of Taxation FAQ).

The Division's home sale guide adds two cautions for movers. Say on the application that you moved after October 1, or the benefit can be lost. Anyone in Senior Freeze who buys another New Jersey home waits two years, instead of three, for a new base year.

Separate local deductions exist for seniors and disabled persons and for veterans, along with an exemption for disabled veterans. Your town's tax office administers those, so ask whether the break on your Morris County house stops at closing.

What happens at the table when a Morris County house sells?

At recording, the seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee and hands in a GIT/REP form with the deed. Someone who stays a New Jersey resident signs GIT/REP-3, which avoids a deposit, and reports any gain on the NJ-1040 afterward. Rates are on the Division's Realty Transfer Fee page.

Deeds are recorded by the Registry Department of the Morris County Clerk. Every land document needs a cover sheet and a cover letter with the submitter's name and address, plus a "Record & Return" or "Cancel & Return" note on the document. Recording runs from 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM at the Registry, whose phone is 973-285-6130.

Request a payoff figure for any unpaid quarter from your town's tax office, and have the closing attorney prorate the current year's bill. Those two numbers decide your net from a Morris County sale.

What does the Morris County job base mean for buyers?

Morris County has 16,518 employer establishments and about 301,249 jobs, with a 2023 payroll near $29.8 billion. Health care and social assistance brought in $6.83 billion in 2022 receipts, and retail sales reached $12.3 billion, or $24,110 per resident. Employment grew 1.9 percent from 2022 to 2023.

A deep local job market means a house that is priced to the county's $582,500 typical value usually draws interest from buyers who already work nearby. A house that needs a roof or an estate cleanout draws fewer offers, which leaves its owner weighing an as is sale against months of repairs.

More questions about Morris County, NJ Property Tax Guide

Where do I file a Morris County property tax appeal?

File with the Morris County Board of Taxation, using Form A-1 and the comparable sales form. The board's mailing address is P.O. Box 900, Morristown, NJ 07963-0900, and hearings take place in person.

What is the deadline for a Morris County tax appeal?

April 1 is the usual receipt date, and May 1 replaces it after a town revaluation or reassessment. Since the Division wants the petition in hand by then, send it well ahead of time.

Does Morris County bill my property tax?

No, your municipality bills and collects it. The county board sets rates and equalization ratios and hears appeals, while your town's tax office issues the bill and supplies payoff figures at a sale.

Can a $1.2 million assessment bypass the county board?

Yes, you may take an assessment above $1,000,000 straight to the Tax Court of New Jersey. The same April 1 or May 1 receipt date governs that filing.

Who pays the transfer fee on a Morris County sale?

The seller pays at recording. A graduated percent fee also falls on the seller if the price goes above $1,000,000.

What we could not confirm

Ocean County by the numbers

Which offices touch a property tax bill in Ocean County?

A house in Ocean County is valued by the town assessor and billed by the town collector. At the county level, the Board of Taxation hears challenges to assessments. The board's own contact page says property tax inquiries go to the tax collector of the municipality where the home sits.

The county has 33 municipalities, from Lakewood and Toms River to small shore boroughs such as Harvey Cedars and Mantoloking. Each one bills on its own schedule inside the state framework, so the first call for any Ocean County seller is the collector in the town that holds the parcel.

  • Ocean County Board of Taxation: Ocean County Court House, Room 215, 118 Washington Street, Toms River, phone (732) 929-2008.
  • Town assessor: value, deductions and exemption forms.
  • Town tax collector: balances, payoff figures and payment options.
  • County Clerk: recording of the deed after a sale.

How big is Ocean County, and who lives in its homes?

Since 2020 no New Jersey county has grown faster than Ocean, which reached an estimated 673,746 people in 2025, a 5.7% gain on 2020. It sits about 70 miles south of New York City and 25 miles north of Atlantic City, and more than 31% of its total area is water, mostly Barnegat Bay and the Atlantic coast.

By the 2020 to 2024 survey, 80.7% of homes were owner-occupied, the median owner-occupied home was valued at $398,400, and median household income was $89,863. Residents 65 or older account for 24.0% of the county, which matters because several state relief programs target older owners. Ocean County issued 2,831 building permits in 2025.

Growth spread unevenly. Lakewood Township had an estimated 139,866 residents in 2023, while Jackson Township covers 100.62 square miles, the largest area of any town. A bayfront bungalow in Brick, a retirement-community home in Manchester and a Lakewood multifamily house can carry very different assessments and very different bills.

What happens when an Ocean County installment is paid late?

The year splits into four installments that fall due on the first day of February, May, August and November. Interest on a late installment is set by town resolution, up to 8% annually on the first $1,500 owed and up to 18% annually on whatever exceeds it.

A town can also allow a ten day grace period before interest starts. Whether a given Ocean County town does so is a local resolution, so ask that town's collector before relying on a grace window. Where a town has adopted one, a delinquency above $10,000 can also bring a year-end penalty of no more than 6% (R.S. 54:4-67).

Unpaid balances can end up in a tax sale. Under R.S. 54:5-19, a town may run an accelerated sale for amounts still unpaid on the 11th day of the eleventh month of the fiscal year. Anyone behind on payments should request a written payoff before listing, since the debt follows the parcel until it is settled.

What steps does an Ocean County assessment appeal follow?

The Ocean County Board of Taxation takes petitions through April 1. A town that finished a citywide revaluation or reassessment gets until May 1 instead, and late-mailed assessment notices stretch the window to 45 days after the bulk mailing. A petition mailed on the last day but received the next one is late, because the board closes at 4:30 p.m.

  • File one petition per parcel and serve a copy on the town assessor and the municipal clerk.
  • Fees scale with assessed value: $5 below $150,000, $25 up to $500,000, $100 up to $1 million and $150 beyond that, by check payable to the Ocean County Treasurer.
  • Deliver up to five comparable sales, plus any appraisal, no later than a week before the hearing.
  • Be current on all taxes through the first quarter of the tax year, as N.J.S.A. 54:3-27 requires.

Only the assessment is on the table. The bill itself comes from budgets, and the assessment is presumed correct until you prove otherwise. A typical hearing begins at nine in the morning. A no-show without written postponement ends in dismissal, and that kind of dismissal cannot be taken to Tax Court. Either side can carry a county judgment to the Tax Court of New Jersey by filing a complaint within 45 days of mailing. Left alone, the judgment is frozen: it binds the assessor for the assessment year and the next two.

What are the Chapter 123 ratios in Ocean County?

Chapter 123 compares your assessment with the true value of the home using a town's average ratio. If your ratio lands outside the 15% common level range around that average, the board resets the assessment. The table shows the tax year 2025 figures the county board published for five towns.

Chapter 123 average ratios, tax year 2025, Ocean County Board of Taxation
MunicipalityAverage ratioLower limitUpper limit
Toms River Township80.2268.1992.25
Brick Township59.1850.3068.06
Lakewood Township56.2847.8464.72
Ocean Township99.3384.43114.23
Jackson Township100.00100.00100.00

Jackson Township is marked as a revaluation town, so its ratio is treated as 100%. Check the board's current published list before you file, because the ratios change each year.

Which tax relief programs can Ocean County owners use?

The state's Division of Taxation runs Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ through one combined application, and the Fiscal Year 2027 budget funds all three. Applications for the 2025 benefit year closed on November 2, 2026; the Division's page lists the next filing period.

  • Senior Freeze reimburses eligible seniors and disabled owners for increases in property tax on a main home.
  • ANCHOR gives relief to owners and renters who live in the property as their main home and meet income limits.
  • Local deductions for veterans, seniors and disabled owners come through the town assessor, and a dispute over a denied deduction can be filed with the county board at no fee.

Because nearly a quarter of residents are 65 or older, many Ocean County sellers hold benefits tied to the home, and the buyer's side should know which ones end at sale.

What county steps follow an Ocean County closing?

Deeds are filed with the Ocean County Clerk. At the Ocean County Clerk's Office a deed costs $45 for its first page and $10 per added page, a mortgage costs $35 to start, and a missing cover sheet adds $20. Payment is by cash, check or escrow account, and checks over $10,000 must be certified.

Ahead of closing, request a tax search and payoff letter from the town collector, and ask the assessor whether a pending appeal, added assessment or deduction affects the next bill. Old tax sale certificates are recorded at the Clerk's Office as well, at $35, and must be redeemed or cancelled for clean title.

More questions about Ocean County, NJ Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay Ocean County property tax?

Payment goes to your own town's tax collector. The board's contact page directs tax questions to the collector for the town that holds the parcel.

When must an Ocean County appeal be filed?

April 1 is the standard cutoff. Towns that just revalued or reassessed get May 1, and notices mailed late stretch either date to 45 days after the bulk mailing. The board closes at 4:30 p.m.

Can I appeal my tax bill in Ocean County?

No. Only the assessed value can be appealed, since taxes come from the budget process. You need sales or an appraisal showing market value on the prior October 1, enough to overcome the presumption that the assessment is right.

What is the filing fee for an Ocean County appeal?

The fee runs from $5 to $150 depending on assessed value. There is no fee to contest the denial of a veteran, senior or disabled deduction.

Can I sell an Ocean County house that has back taxes?

Yes. Arrears and interest come off the seller's side of the closing statement, so ask the town collector for a payoff figure first. A tax sale certificate, if one exists, has to be redeemed before title is clear.

Essex County by the numbers

Who handles property tax for Essex County homeowners?

Essex County has 22 municipalities, and each one has its own assessor and tax collector. The Essex County Board of Taxation sits above them at 495 Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Blvd., Room 230, in Newark, and takes calls at 973-395-8525. Its website, essexcountynjtaxboard.org, carries appeal forms, tax rates, the equalization table, deduction forms and the contact list for every town's assessor and collector.

The county seat is Newark, New Jersey's largest city by population. Bills combine school, municipal and county levies, so identical houses in two Essex towns can receive quite different totals. The board posts pie charts showing how each town's tax dollar is divided.

  • Assessor: sets the assessed value and handles deductions and exemptions.
  • Collector: mails the bill, receives payments and gives payoff figures.
  • County Tax Board: hears appeals and sets the tax rates each year.

How does Essex County look to a seller?

Essex County is small and crowded: 126.09 square miles of land holding about 896,000 people. The ground rises from flat country in the east to the twin Watchung ridges in the western half, topping out near 660 feet around Verona, North Caldwell and Cedar Grove. The lowest point is sea level at Newark Bay.

The east side is anchored by Newark Liberty International Airport, Port Newark and Newark Penn Station, the hub for NJ Transit, whose headquarters sits just behind it. The west side holds the Oranges, Montclair, Verona and the Caldwells. Rutgers University-Newark, the Newark Museum of Art and Thomas Edison National Historical Park draw regular traffic from outside the county.

Essex County figures from the Census Bureau QuickFacts

Population estimate, mid-2025896,379

Fewer than half of Essex households own their home, so renters occupy most housing and many sales involve a tenant in place. Newark's record high of 108 degrees on July 22, 2011 is the hottest reading ever logged in New Jersey, and January lows there average about 24 degrees, so roofs, boilers and cooling systems all get a workout.

When must an Essex County appeal reach the board?

Essex County follows the state calendar: the county board must have your petition in hand on April 1, or by the 45th day after the town finishes mailing assessment notices, whichever is later. Where a town has completed a municipal-wide revaluation or reassessment, the deadline is May 1. Postmarks do not count, and a late petition is dismissed.

If April 1 or May 1 falls on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, the last day moves to the following working day. Owners of property assessed above $1,000,000 may skip the county board and file in the Tax Court of New Jersey, with the same dates. The board's public schedule of meetings and tax appeal hearings is on its website.

How do you prepare and file an Essex County appeal?

Start with the state's Form A-1 and its comparable sales sheet, and file the original with the Essex County Tax Board. The board's site lists its current appeal forms and reminders, and the Division of Taxation has the same forms.

  • Build your case on market value as of October 1 of the pretax year. The appeal covers the assessed value alone.
  • Use up to five comparable sales, each with block, lot, price and deed date. Comparable assessments are not accepted.
  • Check your town's average ratio on the equalization table. If the ratio of assessed to true value falls outside a band of 15 percent around the average, the board adjusts the value using that average ratio.
  • Serve a copy on your municipal assessor and clerk.
  • Attend the hearing yourself or send an attorney, unless you chose a summary hearing on written evidence.

If the board turns you down, the Tax Court in Trenton takes a complaint filed within 45 days of the judgment. A board judgment holds for the year and the two after it unless a revaluation or added assessment changes the picture.

What happens at an Essex County Tax Board hearing?

You pick the format on the petition: an in-person hearing, a virtual hearing if the county offers one, or a summary hearing decided only on the papers you send. A summary hearing means you cannot explain your comparables aloud, so every sale you rely on has to be clearly like your house. Homeowners may speak for themselves, while an LLC, trust or corporation needs a New Jersey attorney unless the property's prior-year tax was under $25,000.

  • Filing fee is $5 for assessed value under $150,000, $25 up to $500,000, $100 up to $1,000,000 and $150 above that, paid by check to the County Tax Administrator and not refundable.
  • Adjournments are granted only for extraordinary reasons.
  • The town may cross-appeal, and you will be told and invited to attend.
  • If you rely on an appraisal, the appraiser has to appear and the report goes to the board at least seven days before the hearing.

How are Essex County tax installments and late interest handled?

Bills in New Jersey are paid in four quarterly installments on February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1, and many towns allow a 10-day grace period. Late payments pick up interest back to the original due date, at 8 percent on the first $1,500 and 18 percent beyond that. A delinquency over $10,000 left open at year end can also draw a penalty of up to 6 percent.

In Edison, for example, a balance still open on November 11 can go into the town's tax sale, and Essex towns run their own sales on the same state framework. A town lien blocks the sale of the house until it is redeemed. The collector can quote the exact payoff, and a title company will want it before closing.

  • Get a payoff letter from the collector that states the daily interest.
  • Confirm whether the water or sewer account is separate from the tax account.
  • Pay the installment that falls during your closing window, or make sure the title company withholds it.

What relief programs help Essex County owners?

The state's fiscal year 2027 budget pays for Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ. The 2025 application closed on November 2, 2026, so look at the Division of Taxation page for the next one. The municipal assessor handles the $250 deductions for qualified veterans, seniors and disabled owners, and the full exemption for a 100 percent disabled veteran, and the Essex board lists those forms online. Eligibility is measured as of October 1 of the year before the tax year, and the senior and disabled deduction carries an income ceiling of $10,000 that leaves out certain Social Security and pension income. If a town denies a deduction, you can appeal that denial to the county board without paying a filing fee.

More questions about Essex County, NJ Property Tax Guide

Where do I send an Essex County property tax appeal?

Send it to the Essex County Board of Taxation, 495 Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Blvd., Room 230, Newark, NJ 07102. Call 973-395-8525 to check the hearing schedule and filing method.

What if my town just had a revaluation?

The deadline moves from April 1 to May 1 for that year. The board and your municipal assessor can confirm whether your town qualifies.

Is a late Essex County appeal ever accepted?

No. The petition has to be received by the end of business on the deadline date, and the board dismisses late filings.

Do I keep paying tax while an appeal is open?

Yes. You must stay current through the first quarter at least, and the board may relax that rule when justice requires.

Can an Essex County house sell with tax still owed?

Yes. The unpaid tax, interest and any lien are cleared from the seller's money at the table, so request a payoff letter from the municipal collector first.

Hudson County by the numbers

What makes Hudson County's property tax system different?

Hudson ranks as New Jersey's smallest county by land and its most crowded, and each of its twelve municipalities keeps its own assessor and tax collector inside that compact map. The county itself supplies the Board of Taxation, which hears assessment appeals, and a Division of Tax Assessments that supports it. Bills come from the city or town where the house stands, and a single bill folds in municipal, school and county levies.

The county is bordered by the Hudson River and Upper New York Bay on the east and by Newark Bay and the Hackensack and Passaic rivers on the west. Its only land border is with Bergen County. Much of the shoreline was built on reclaimed land, and the Palisades rise in the north.

Which Hudson County offices should a homeowner know?

The Division of Tax Assessments is part of the county's finance department, while the county Board of Taxation keeps legal oversight of it and the County Tax Administrator runs the division day to day. The office is at Hudson County Plaza, 257 Cornelison Avenue, 3rd Floor, Jersey City, NJ 07302, and the phone is (201) 395-6260.

  • Appeals: petitions can be filed through the county's online appeal filing system, handed in at the office, requested at the counter, or mailed out after a call.
  • Relief applications: one combined application covers Senior Freeze reimbursement, ANCHOR, the Stay NJ credit, deductions, exemptions and abatements.
  • Records search: assessment records are searched through a free system run by the county clerk's records management office.
  • Bills and payments: these go to the municipal tax collector, not the county.

Hudson is one of two New Jersey counties with an elected Register of Deeds, so deeds in this county are recorded through that office. Confirm its current counter details before you schedule a closing.

What are the 2025 tax rates across Hudson County?

Two figures appear for every district. The general rate is charged on assessed value in hundred-dollar units, and the effective rate restates it against estimated true value. The two can differ widely: Kearny shows a general rate of 10.848 yet an effective rate of 1.985. Use the effective column when you compare towns.

How does a Hudson County assessment appeal work?

An owner petitions the county board by April 1 (or 45 days after notices go out in bulk), and May 1 replaces that date once a town has revalued or reassessed. October 1 of the year before the tax year is the state's assessment date, and the board weighs true market value against the assessed figure.

  • The taxpayer has to prove the value, and sales used as evidence should predate October 1.
  • The common level range is plus or minus 15 percent of the district's average ratio, and it is the test of fairness when assessments are not updated every year.
  • The board must decide appeals within three months of the last filing day, and hearings usually occur within that window.
  • The assessments of similar properties are not usable evidence. Sales of comparable homes are.
  • A denied senior or disabled deduction is appealed on Form A-1 by April 1 after the denial.

Appeals are also possible in the state's Tax Court. Burlington, Gloucester and Monmouth counties follow a January 15 deadline instead, which does not apply here.

Which relief programs does Hudson County point owners toward?

The county division names Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ among its relief programs on one combined application. A separate $250 deduction exists for homeowners who are 65 or older or disabled, with one year of New Jersey residence before October 1 and an income limit. Surviving spouses and civil union partners age 55 or older can keep it on the same home. The renewal form goes to the tax collector by March 1 every year.

Anyone selling an inherited house should check whether a deceased owner's deduction still sits on the account, and ask the assessor what the new owner must file.

Source: NJ Division of Taxation; Hudson County Division of Tax Assessments.

What do Census numbers show for Hudson County?

Federal estimates give Hudson 735,033 residents for 2025, a 1.4 percent rise over the 724,854 counted in 2020. Housing totals 327,344 units for 299,682 households, and owners live in only 30.7 percent. Homes they own were valued at a median $539,700 for 2020 to 2024, with median rent at $1,894 and median household income at $91,795.

Foreign-born residents are 42.8 percent of the population, and 56.5 percent of residents five and older use another language at home. Builders took out 3,352 permits in 2025, and commuters average 35.4 minutes each way. Squeezing that many people into 46.19 square miles of land (15,691.5 per square mile) means one block can differ sharply from the next, so these are county-wide averages.

Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts.

How do Hudson County towns fit together for sellers?

North Hudson holds Union City, West New York, Weehawken, Guttenberg and North Bergen along the Palisades. Jersey City and Bayonne run down the peninsula to the south, Hoboken sits along the central waterfront, and the western side around Harrison, East Newark, Kearny and Secaucus borders the Hackensack and Passaic rivers and the Meadowlands. Jersey City is the county seat, and the courthouse and administration building stand on Newark Avenue near Five Corners.

Transit shapes demand: Hoboken Terminal, Journal Square, Exchange Place and Secaucus Junction anchor rail and PATH service, and the Holland and Lincoln tunnels lead to Manhattan. Because every town sets its own assessments and collects its own bills, a seller should ask the specific municipal collector about unpaid quarters and any lien before anything else.

What happens at a Hudson County sale when tax is still owed?

Under N.J.S.A. 54:4-66 a quarter that passes its delinquency date stays delinquent until every unpaid tax, later lien and the interest are paid. A closing therefore has to carry the exact payoff, and that number changes by the day. Collectors in the county's twelve towns issue the figure, and one of them warns that lien balances posted online can be wrong, so a written statement beats a screen.

The deed also brings a state transfer fee at the recording counter. The fee schedule comes from state law and is the same in every county, so ask the recording office which price band your sale falls in and whether an exemption fits.

More questions about Hudson County, NJ Property Tax Guide

Which board decides assessment appeals in Hudson County?

The county's Board of Taxation decides them, from offices at Hudson County Plaza on Cornelison Avenue in Jersey City. Call (201) 395-6260 for forms.

What is the deadline to appeal a Hudson County assessment?

Usually April 1. A town that has revalued or reassessed moves it to May 1.

Which Hudson County town has the lowest effective tax rate?

Hoboken posts 1.070 in the state's 2025 table, and Guttenberg posts the highest at 2.435.

Does the county collect my property tax bill?

No. Your own city or town collects the bill, and the county's role stops at appeals and relief paperwork.

Can I sell a Hudson County house that has back taxes?

Yes, with the balance and interest cleared at or before closing. Request a written payoff from your town's collector.

Camden County by the numbers

Who does what on property tax in Camden County?

Three layers share the work in Camden County. Value comes from the town assessor, the bill and the money move through the town collector, and disputes over value go to the Camden County Board of Taxation. The board sits at 509 Lakeland Road in Blackwood, has public hours on weekdays from 9 to 4 and a phone line at 856-225-5238.

A single bill covers several taxing bodies. In Cherry Hill, the county's most populous town, the township's own 2026 breakdown shows the county levy at 18.86 percent of an average bill, with the school district taking the biggest share. Owners in the other towns see a different mix, so the back of your bill is the place to check your own split.

  • A change of name or mailing address is requested in writing at the municipal assessor's office.
  • Questions about how much you owe or when it is due go to your town's tax collector.
  • A value you think is too high becomes a case for the county board, once you have spoken with your assessor.

What is Camden County like beyond the tax bill?

The land area of Camden County is 221.36 square miles, stretched along the Delaware River, directly across from Philadelphia, and its ground is flat and low. Its highest surveyed point is about 219 feet above sea level. Camden city, chartered in 1828, serves as the seat, and 36 municipalities share the county, from dense river towns to the wooded suburbs near Voorhees and Cherry Hill.

For July 2025 the Census Bureau counts 535,799 residents, compared with 523,500 in April 2020. Typical home value runs about $287,100, about 64.7 percent of households own, and the middle household earns $88,755 a year. The home value sits well below the $524,100 median in Essex County, so price a Camden County house against nearby local sales.

  • Employers include Campbell's and Subaru of America, both headquartered in the county, plus medical schools run with Rowan University in Camden and Stratford.
  • The county became the first in the nation to require recycling, in 1985, and its sustainability work targets stormwater and flooding.
  • The PATCO Speedline runs from Philadelphia through Camden to Lindenwold, with stops at Woodcrest, Westmont and Collingswood.
  • Low, flat ground and an aging storm drain system leave parts of the county exposed to flooding, which buyers and inspectors look at closely.

When can you appeal a Camden County assessment?

Petitions are accepted from the time assessment notices go out until the 4 p.m. close on April 1, or the 45th day after the town finishes its notice mailing, whichever is later. A petition still in the mail at that hour is late. A postmark does not count, and a late petition is dismissed.

Towns that have just finished a revaluation or reassessment get a one-month extension to May 1. The board's website names the towns in that position for the current cycle, and a deadline falling on a Sunday or legal holiday slides to the following working day. Bills for added or omitted assessments, which come from new construction or an error on the tax list, follow their own December 1 rule.

Camden County Board of Taxation filing rules, per the board's own instructions
SituationRule
Regular appealDelivered before the 4 p.m. close on April 1, or on the 45th day after notices go out if that is later
Town revalued or reassessedDelivered before the 4 p.m. close on May 1
Added or omitted assessmentIn hand by December 1, or a month after the collector mails those bills if that is later
Comparable sales evidenceAt the board, assessor and clerk at least 7 days before the hearing
Further appealTax Court of New Jersey, filed inside 45 days of the judgment

How do you file an appeal with the Camden County board?

Petitions can be sent through the board's online portal, by post, or delivered by hand, and hearings run in a virtual format alongside the Blackwood meeting room. Online filing runs through a site the board names on its appeals page, which works best in Chrome, Safari or Firefox. The paper form is on the board's forms page.

  • Each parcel needs its own petition and fee: $5 under $150,000 of assessed value, $25 up to $500,000, $100 up to $1,000,000, and $150 above that.
  • Give your town's assessor and clerk their own copies.
  • Use up to five comparable sales, with block, lot, sale price and deed date. Comparable assessments do not count as evidence.
  • Keep paying installments during the case, at the very least through the first quarter, unless the board eases that requirement.

The appeal covers the assessed value alone, and the number the board wants proven is market value on the October 1 that precedes the tax year. If the board lowers your value, the judgment is held in place for that year and the next two unless something such as a town revaluation changes it.

Can a Camden County house sell while tax is still owed?

Back tax does not disappear at sale, because it stays with the property until someone pays it. New Jersey towns charge 8 percent a year on the initial $1,500 owed and 18 percent on the rest, counted back to the due date once the grace period passes. Cherry Hill, for example, gives a 10-day grace period and refuses postmarks.

If a town sells a tax lien on your property, the house cannot be sold until the lien is redeemed. A buyer who holds the lien can start foreclosure in state court if it stays open for two years. Before signing a sale contract, ask your town collector for a payoff in writing, with interest calculated to a named day.

  • Pass the latest bill to the buyer or title company.
  • Check sewer and water accounts separately, because many towns bill them apart from the tax.
  • Several quarters behind? Ask for the payoff early so the closing agent has time to plan.

Which tax relief programs reach Camden County homeowners?

Three state relief programs, Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ, are funded in the fiscal year 2027 budget for owners and renters. Applications for 2025 were due November 2, 2026, which has passed, and the Division of Taxation's relief page carries the next window.

Locally, the municipal assessor takes the state-mandated deductions: $250 for qualifying veterans, $250 for seniors and disabled owners who meet the income limit, and a full exemption for owners with a 100 percent permanent and total service-connected disability. Each has residency and ownership tests measured on the prior October 1. Ask your town assessor for the current application.

More questions about Camden County, NJ Property Tax Guide

Which office takes a Camden County assessment appeal?

The board at 509 Lakeland Road, Blackwood, NJ 08012, accepts petitions online, by mail or at the counter. Call 856-225-5238 with questions, and give your town assessor and clerk a copy.

Does the April 1 appeal date ever change?

Yes. Towns that completed a revaluation or reassessment use May 1 instead. In every case the petition has to reach the board before it closes for the day on the final date.

Does an appeal lower my tax bill right away?

No. You keep paying your installments, at least through the first quarter, while the case is pending. A reduction in value carries into later bills and any overpayment is dealt with after judgment.

Can I sell with back taxes owed?

Yes. Tax, interest and any lien are settled from the money the seller receives at closing. A written payoff from your town collector should be in hand before you pick a closing date.

Who sets Camden County tax rates?

Each town's rate comes from the combined school, municipal, county and any special district levies divided by the town's total assessed value. The county board of taxation sets the rate, and your municipal collector bills it.

Middlesex County by the numbers

Where is Middlesex County, NJ, and which towns does it hold?

Middlesex County sits in central New Jersey, running from the Raritan Valley toward the northern end of the Jersey Shore. Wikipedia reports 322.87 square miles in total, with 309.22 of them land, and describes a largely flat county bisected by the Raritan River. The county seat is New Brunswick, home of Rutgers University.

The county government counts twenty-five municipalities. Edison is the largest, with 107,588 residents in 2020, and Monroe Township covers the most ground at 42.19 square miles. Woodbridge Township holds the junction of the New Jersey Turnpike and the Garden State Parkway, and East Brunswick contains the state's center of population. Other towns include Perth Amboy, South Amboy, South Brunswick, Metuchen and South Plainfield.

Since the county is large and varied, a house in a Raritan Bay town such as South Amboy and one in a Route 1 corridor township such as South Brunswick are billed by different municipalities and school districts, even though the same county board rules on their appeals.

Which offices run property tax in Middlesex County?

Middlesex County does not send most homeowners a tax bill. In each of the twenty-five towns, a local assessor values property and a local collector sends the bill, and the county tax board supervises that work and hears appeals. Your town's collector is the person to ask for payment help and payoff numbers.

The Middlesex County Board of Taxation lists these basics:

  • Location: County Administration Building, 4th Floor, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick, NJ 08901.
  • Phone: 732-745-3350. The office opens weekdays from 8:30 AM until 4:15 PM.
  • Duties: certifying assessments and municipal tax rates, equalizing assessments for county taxes, preparing the abstract of ratables, supervising local assessors and hearing appeals.

The board explains that county tax boards were created by legislation in 1909 and that all 21 of them follow a uniform set of rules written by the state Division of Taxation. Five commissioners sit on the Middlesex board, and the county tax administrator runs the daily office.

What are the Middlesex County assessment appeal deadlines?

Regular petitions must be received by April 1, or within 45 days after assessment notices are mailed in bulk, and May 1 applies where a town carried out a revaluation or reassessment. The state's guide to tax appeal hearings gives those dates, and Middlesex is not one of the three counties on the alternate calendar.

Other practical points from the county tax board:

  • Petitions can be filed through the board's online portal after creating an account, and the portal issues proof of filing.
  • The petition is forwarded to the board, the municipal assessor and the municipal clerk.
  • Evidence can be uploaded at filing or up to seven calendar days before the hearing, by 4:00 PM.
  • The deadline for added and omitted assessment appeals in 2026 was December 1.
  • The board resolved against virtual hearings.

An appeal covers the assessment only. The state guide notes that taxes come from local budgets and cannot be appealed, and it describes the common level range, which is plus or minus 15% of the director's ratio for the town. It also explains the freeze act, which holds an appealed value for the assessment year and the next two years unless something changes the property.

How does Middlesex County compare with its neighbors on housing and income?

Middlesex County is dense and diverse, and its home values trail those of neighboring Monmouth County. Census QuickFacts shows the following for the 2020-2024 survey period unless noted.

Middlesex County and Monmouth County, Census Bureau QuickFacts
MeasureMiddlesex CountyMonmouth County
Population estimate, July 2025883,335651,035
Owner-occupied housing rate63.6%75.6%
Median home value$462,900$606,100
Median household income$111,549$124,845
Median gross rent$1,871$1,827
Land area, square miles309.22468.18

More than a third of Middlesex households rent, and the county reports 2,791.4 people per square mile. For sellers, that means a large pool of condominium and multifamily properties alongside single-family houses, and a lot of buyers who commute by rail or turnpike.

What is the land and climate like across Middlesex County?

The county is flat to gently rolling. Wikipedia puts elevations between sea level and about 300 feet, with the high ground near Route 1 in South Brunswick and a moraine ridge stretching through Perth Amboy, Woodbridge, Edison and Metuchen. Clay was mined along the Raritan Formation until the late twentieth century, especially near Woodbridge.

The climate is hot-summer humid continental, bordering humid subtropical along Raritan Bay and the Arthur Kill. New Brunswick averages 31.9 degrees Fahrenheit in January and 75.6 in July, and monthly precipitation runs from 2.98 inches in February to 5.08 inches in July. Wet summers and freezing winters are normal here, so roofs, gutters and basements are routine items on a buyer's inspection list.

Which employers and transport links shape the Middlesex County market?

The county's economy runs on health care, education, pharmaceuticals, finance and logistics. Wikipedia lists Rutgers University as the largest non-governmental employer, followed by Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital, and names Bristol-Myers Squibb, Wakefern Food Corporation, Johnson & Johnson, Prudential and several other hospitals among the large employers. The Bureau of Economic Analysis put the county's gross domestic product at $59.0 billion in 2021, second in New Jersey.

Transport matters just as much. Several stations on NJ Transit's Northeast Corridor Line serve the county, and the Turnpike and Parkway meet in Woodbridge. Census data puts the average commute at 31.2 minutes. Ask the assessor in your town how commute access is reflected in the value on your record.

What should a Middlesex County seller do about unpaid property tax?

Start with the collector in the municipality where the house stands, because the county does not collect. Ask for a written payoff through the expected closing date, and ask whether the town has sold a tax lien on the parcel. New Jersey law makes the owner responsible for the tax even without a bill, and statewide, four installments come due each year, at the start of February, May, August and November.

If you plan to appeal, remember that the appeal must be filed by April 1 (May 1 after a revaluation), and that the first quarter's taxes and municipal charges are normally required to be paid for an appeal to proceed. Contact the county tax board at 732-745-3350 with questions about a pending petition, because the outcome can lower the value that a buyer sees on the record.

Relief programs also change with a sale. The state's relief page lists the three benefits, Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ, and notes that the deadline for the 2025 application was November 2, 2026.

More questions about Middlesex County, NJ Property Tax Guide

Where does a Middlesex County owner send an assessment petition?

File with the Middlesex County Board of Taxation, which accepts petitions online and at 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. Each petition is passed on to the municipal assessor and clerk.

What is the standard appeal deadline in Middlesex County?

April 1, or within 45 days after bulk-mailed assessment notices, with May 1 for towns that completed a revaluation or reassessment. Added and omitted assessment appeals for 2026 were due December 1.

Does Middlesex County collect my property taxes?

No. Your municipal tax collector mails the bill and accepts the payment, and the county board of taxation supervises assessments and hears appeals. Contact the collector in your town for a payoff figure.

How many municipalities are in Middlesex County?

There are twenty-five. They include Edison, Woodbridge, New Brunswick, East Brunswick, Monroe, Perth Amboy and South Brunswick, and each one runs its own assessment and collection offices.

Can I attend a Middlesex County tax appeal hearing by video?

No. The county board of taxation passed a resolution that it will not hold virtual tax appeal hearings, so plan to attend in person or send your evidence ahead of time.

Passaic County by the numbers

Which offices handle property tax in Passaic County, NJ?

Passaic County splits the work between its 16 municipalities and one county board. Each town assessor values property and each town collector bills it. The Passaic County Board of Taxation, created by legislation in 1909, certifies assessments, equalizes values for county tax purposes, prepares the abstract of ratables, certifies municipal tax rates and hears assessment appeals.

  • Board of Taxation: 930 Riverview Drive, Suite 250, Totowa, NJ 07512, phone (973) 720-7399.
  • Appeal hearings: 930 Riverview Drive, Suite 200, Totowa, starting at 9 a.m.
  • Town assessor: valuation, deductions, added and omitted assessments.
  • Town collector: bills, payments and tax payoff letters for a sale.

A Passaic County seller should begin with the collector in the house's own town, because the county board neither bills nor collects.

What makes Passaic County different from other New Jersey counties?

Passaic County is small and dense. Its 186.01 square miles of land hold about 2,818 people per square mile (2020 Census), nearly three times the density of Ocean County. The 2025 Census estimate is 531,624 residents in 186,341 housing units.

The county was created on February 7, 1837 from parts of Bergen and Essex counties. Its southeastern half is flat or gently hilly along the Passaic and Pompton Rivers, while the northwest is rugged highland, with West Milford covering 80.32 square miles, more than 40% of the county's area. Paterson, the county seat, holds more than 30% of the population.

In the 2020 to 2024 survey, owners lived in 53.1% of homes, the median home was worth $459,500 and the median household earned $87,522. One resident in three was born abroad, and just over half of residents age 5 and up use another language at home. Business activity is steady: the county had 12,406 employer establishments and 146,956 jobs in 2023, and 12.1% of residents lived below the poverty line. Builders pulled 585 permits in 2025, far fewer than Ocean County's 2,831. Within one county a seller might hold a two-family house, a rental building or a hillside single-family home, and the tax picture differs for each.

What are the Passaic County tax appeal deadlines?

The board's 2026 notice told owners to wait for the assessment card, which means filing from February 1, and to get a regular petition in by April 1. A town that has just revalued or reassessed gets until May 1; for 2026 the county named Paterson. Added and omitted assessments have their own later deadline.

Passaic County Board of Taxation filing dates for the 2026 appeal year
Type of appealWho it coversLast day to file
Regular petitionMost townsApril 1, 2026
Regular petition after revaluation or reassessmentPaterson for 2026May 1, 2026
Added or omitted assessmentAll 16 municipalitiesDecember 1, 2026

The same pattern repeats each year, so the dates for later years follow the April 1, May 1 and December 1 rule.

How does a Passaic County appeal work once it is filed?

What can be challenged is the assessed value. The rate cannot, and the owner must show what the house was worth the prior October 1.

  • Bring recent sales of similar homes near the October 1 date, with photographs and a property record card from the town assessor.
  • Above $1,000,000 of assessed value, the owner may skip the board and file in state Tax Court.
  • A dissatisfied owner has 45 days after the judgment to go to Tax Court.
  • Added or omitted assessment bills are generally mailed in October and payable November 1, and an appeal of one must be filed before December 1.

Paterson's assessor page lays out the statewide added assessment rule: work finished after October 1 is valued as of the next month's first day and taxed for the whole months left in that year. A seller who built a new deck, a finished basement or an extension should expect the assessor to notice.

How do roads and rivers shape a Passaic County sale?

Interstate 80 and Interstate 287 cross the county near Paterson, and the Garden State Parkway cuts across the southern end near Clifton. The Passaic River is the county's main waterway, and the southeastern half of the county is flat or only mildly hilly along it and the Pompton River. From Totowa the Passaic River runs into Paterson and then south toward Newark, and the county's lowest ground, about 20 feet above sea level, lies along it in Clifton.

Paterson's January lows average 19 degrees and July highs reach 86, with roughly 2.9 to 4.8 inches of rain a month, so roofs, gutters and basements take wear. A seller in a river town does well to gather repair records and any flood history before the first showing. Ask the town building department about open permits before you list.

What happens to unpaid Passaic County property tax?

Each town sets its own late interest within the state ceiling. Debt left open at the close of the fiscal year leads to a standard tax sale the year after, and debt still open on November 11 of the fiscal year can lead to an accelerated sale. The statute lets a town leave out of the sale any property whose owner is paying a signed plan in equal monthly installments that clears the debt within five years.

A town may also add a year-end penalty, capped at 6%, to any delinquency above $10,000. Interest runs daily, so a seller who owes should ask the collector for the exact figure on the closing date.

Relief programs run through the state, and one application covers Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ. Its 2025 round closed November 2, 2026, so the Division of Taxation page is the place to find the next cycle.

What does recording a Passaic County sale cost?

Deeds and mortgages are recorded by the Passaic County Clerk. Its Registry fee list charges $45 for the first page of a deed plus $10 per extra page, $35 to open a mortgage, and $20 for a notice of settlement naming two parties. A mortgage cancellation is $25, and an inheritance tax waiver is $15. Veterans' discharge papers record at no fee, and a certified copy of a recorded document costs $10 for the first page and $2 for each page after.

The same schedule publishes a realty transfer tax table. In the bracket for prices up to $350,000, the first $150,000 is taxed at $4.00 per $1,000, the next $50,000 at $6.70, and the rest up to $350,000 at $7.80. Above $350,000 the rates start at $5.80 per $1,000 and climb in steps to $12.10 per $1,000 above $1,000,000. Senior citizen rates are lower. Your closing agent will confirm which column applies.

More questions about Passaic County, NJ Property Tax Guide

Where is the Passaic County Board of Taxation?

It is at 930 Riverview Drive, Suite 250, Totowa, NJ 07512, and the phone is (973) 720-7399. Appeal hearings are held in Suite 200 at the same address, starting at 9 a.m.

When is the Passaic County tax appeal deadline?

A regular petition is due April 1. A revalued or reassessed town (Paterson in 2026) gets May 1, and added or omitted assessments close December 1. Wait for the assessment card before filing.

Who pays property tax in Passaic County, the county or the town?

You pay your town's tax collector. The county board certifies and hears appeals, but the town bills and collects for municipal, school and county levies together.

Can I appeal a Passaic County assessment on my own?

Yes. Individual owners may represent themselves at the county board, while business entities other than sole proprietorships need an attorney. Properties assessed above $1,000,000 may bypass the board.

Can I sell a Passaic County house with tax owing?

Yes. The collector's payoff letter fixes the number the closing agent remits, interest included. Also ask the town whether a tax sale certificate has been issued on the parcel.
